To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the migration inhibitory factor of rat spleen cells is impaired in the presence of ethanol.

1) ethanol inhibits migration inhibitory factor production in the spleen of rats in vivo; 2) this inhibition is not a direct effect of ethanol, since the ethanol-treated spleen cells are not impaired in their ability to produce migration inhibitory factor in culture; and 3) ethanol inhibits the production of migration inhibitory activity by the spleen in vivo because of a direct action of ethanol on the liver.
ethanol impairs the ability of rat peritoneal exudate cells to respond to lymphokines and that this is due to a direct action of ethanol on the target cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of ethanol on the host response to infection and with the mechanisms by which ethanol alters the host response to microbial challenge.
the role of ethanol and its metabolites in the regulation of soluble mediators of the immune response.
the effects of ethanol on the host inflammatory response and with the possible mechanism for the observed changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ethanol impairs the immune system, but the mechanism is not clear.
ethanol and/or ethanol metabolites can alter the host response to infection by altering the activity of soluble mediators of the inflammatory response.
the effects of ethanol on lymphokine activity are poorly understood, and that further research in this area is needed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ethanol and its metabolites, acetaldehyde and acetate, can alter the production and/or activity of soluble mediators of the immune response.
ethanol impairs lymphokine activity in a dose-dependent and reversible manner.
ethanol and its metabolites may alter the production of lymphokines by T lymphocytes, which in turn may alter the activity of macrophages.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethanol may alter the host response to infection by interfering with the ability of lymphocytes to respond to mediators that normally modulate the inflammatory response.
the effects of ethanol are not limited to the immune cells themselves, but may also involve the soluble mediators of immune response.
alcohol impairs the ability of the host to mount an effective response to infection.
